title: A View From Somewhere: Human-Centric Face Representations

en.text: When a team wants to check whether a face dataset is diverse, the reflex is to reach for demographic labels: race, gender, age. It is the default move across the field, and it rests on shaky ground. Those labels are frequently missing, legally restricted to collect, and unreliable the moment a model or a human annotator has to infer them rather than read them off a record.

They also flatten something that is not flat. "Skin tone" collapses into light or dark; two faces filed under the same category can look nothing alike; and rigid taxonomies erase multi-ethnic people and cause real harm when someone is mislabeled. The deeper issue is not a badly chosen taxonomy that a better one would fix. It is the premise that human appearance sorts cleanly into discrete boxes at all.

A View From Somewhere (AVFS), an ICLR 2023 paper from Sony AI and the University of Tokyo, starts from the opposite premise. Instead of labeling faces, it asks people a simpler question: given three faces, which one is the odd one out? The authors collect 638,180 of these judgments over 4,921 faces and learn a continuous embedding space aligned with human perception, with no demographic label anywhere in the training signal.

en.caption: Figure 2. What a learned dimension looks like. The highest-scoring faces along one AVFS dimension, with the human-generated topic labels (top) and the CelebA / FairFace attributes (bottom) that independently line up with it. Faces are synthetic StyleGAN3 images used for privacy.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17176 — Code: https://github.com/SonyAI/a_view_from_somewhere
Why demographic labels are the wrong measuring stick

Categorical labels answer the wrong question. They can tell you a face is filed as one group or another, but they cannot say how similar two faces within that group are, and similarity is what diversity auditing actually cares about. Human appearance varies continuously, and the same face can strike two observers differently, so any fixed label is a lossy, observer-blind compression of what people actually perceive.

Earlier work tried to learn perceptual embeddings of faces from human judgments, but ran into two walls. Some methods can only place the exact stimuli they were trained on and cannot embed a new face at all. Others pool every judgment into one average observer, discarding the variation within and between annotators — precisely the signal that tells you similarity depends on who is looking. AVFS is designed to break through both walls at once.
The method: odd-one-out judgments and a mask per annotator

The data comes from an odd-one-out task (a triplet judgment): shown three faces, an annotator picks the one least similar to the other two. This forces a relative comparison rather than an absolute label, and it is cognitively easy to do consistently. Crucially, every one of the 638,180 judgments is stamped with the identity and self-reported demographics of the annotator who made it, so the dataset records not just what was judged but who judged it.

On top of this data sits a conditional model. A ResNet18 convnet maps each face to a 128-dimensional embedding. Each annotator is given a learnable gating vector that, after a sigmoid, scales the importance of every embedding dimension for that person. Similarity between two faces is then the dot product of their masked, rectified embeddings, and the model predicts the odd-one-out probability from the three pairwise similarities in a triplet. Formally the per-annotator similarity is sim_a(i,j) = (σ(φ_a) ⊙ ReLU(w_i)) · (σ(φ_a) ⊙ ReLU(w_j)), where φ_a is annotator a's mask and w_i is the embedding of face i.

Two design choices make the space usable rather than just accurate. Setting every mask to ones removes the conditioning and recovers a single unconditional space (AVFS-U); keeping the masks gives the conditional variants AVFS-C and the post-hoc AVFS-CPH. And a sparsity-plus-non-negativity penalty pushes most dimensions to zero, leaving roughly 22 active, non-negative dimensions that a person can actually read — the paper retains 22 interpretable dimensions at 61.9% validation accuracy. Figure 2 above shows one such dimension: its top faces, the words humans used to describe it, and the CelebA/FairFace attributes that independently track it all agree, which is what "interpretable" means here.
Does a perception-aligned space actually predict human judgment?

The first test holds out judgments over the same faces the model was trained on — 24,060 of them — and asks the model to predict which face humans called the odd one out. Figure 1 reports accuracy across models. Representations trained on semantic labels (FairFace, CelebA, FFHQ, CASIA-WebFace) sit in the low-to-mid 50% range, while the AVFS models climb well past them; even an AVFS-U variant trained on just 12.5% of the judgments still beats every semantic baseline.

en.caption: Figure 1. Predicting similarity on held-out judgments over the same 24,060 faces. Semantic-label representations (left) trail every AVFS model (right); even AVFS-U-12.5% stays ahead of the baselines.

en.text: The harder test uses 80,300 judgments over entirely novel faces the model never saw in training. This is where a merely memorized space would fall apart. Instead, as Figure 3 shows, the AVFS models again lead the semantic baselines, and the annotator-specific masks continue to help even on unfamiliar faces — evidence that the masks capture something transferable about how a given person judges similarity, not just a fit to the training stimuli.

en.caption: Figure 3. Predicting similarity on 80,300 judgments over novel faces. The conditional models (AVFS-C, AVFS-CPH) generalize to triplets built entirely from unseen faces.

en.text: The table below distills both tests. Across same-stimuli and novel-stimuli accuracy, the AVFS models improve on the best semantic baseline by roughly six to twelve points, and they do it without ever seeing a demographic label during training.

en.caption: Table 1. Odd-one-out accuracy (%), best semantic baseline vs AVFS models.

en.text: Do annotators really matter, or is the mask decoration?

If every person judged similarity the same way, the annotator masks would be interchangeable and swapping them at random would cost nothing. The authors test exactly that: they randomly reassign which annotator mask is attached to each of the 80,300 novel-stimuli judgments and recompute accuracy 100 times. The best conditional model's accuracy falls from 61.7% to 52.8% — a large, consistent drop showing who does the judging is part of the signal.

A second analysis eliminates embedding dimensions one at a time. Only 6–13 dimensions are needed to recover 95–99% of the predictive accuracy, but 15–22 are required to explain 95–99% of the full similarity structure. Which dimensions matter, in other words, depends on the context of each particular comparison.

en.caption: Figure 4. Annotator positionality. A linear SVM can separate annotator masks by demographic group well above chance (the horizontal line), so sociocultural background leaves a measurable trace in how people judge face similarity.

en.text: Figure 4 makes the same point from the other direction. A simple linear classifier can tell annotators apart by demographic group from their masks alone, with every confidence interval clear of chance. The model never trained on those group labels; the structure emerged because different people genuinely weigh visual dimensions differently. The paper is careful here — this is a description of how judgments vary, not an endorsement of any grouping as ground truth.
Why it matters

AVFS trades a demographic label for a record of who judged what, and gets back a continuous, interpretable, perception-aligned face representation that measures diversity without forcing people into discrete boxes. For teams constrained by law and ethics on collecting sensitive attributes, that is a practical alternative, not just a philosophical one.

The boundaries are worth keeping in view: the faces are near-frontal and the annotator pool, though diverse, is finite. But the framework only needs to know who made which judgment, so nothing about it is specific to faces — the same recipe could learn perception-aligned representations for almost any task built on human comparison. That generality is what makes the paper worth reading.

zh.text: 要判断一个人脸数据集是否「足够多样」，业界的第一反应几乎总是去看人口统计标签（demographic labels）：种族、性别、年龄。这个默认做法其实站得并不稳。这类标签常常是缺失的，采集上又受到法律限制，而一旦需要靠模型或标注者去「推断」而不是直接读取，它就变得很不可靠。
更根本的问题在于，这些标签把本来连续的东西压成了离散的格子。「肤色」被简化成深或浅；被归到同一类别的两张脸，看上去可能毫无相似之处；而僵硬的分类体系会抹去多族裔个体的存在，一旦贴错标签还可能造成真实的心理伤害。问题不在于某个分类体系没选好、换一个更好的就能解决，而在于「人的外貌可以被干净地装进离散盒子」这个前提本身。
ICLR 2023 上来自 Sony AI 与东京大学的论文 A View From Somewhere（AVFS，「来自某处的视角」）选择了相反的前提。它不去给人脸贴标签，而是问一个更朴素的问题：给你三张脸，哪一张是「最不像」的那一个？作者收集了 638,180 次这样的判断，覆盖 4,921 张人脸，并据此学习出一个与人类感知对齐的连续嵌入空间——训练信号里没有出现任何一个人口统计标签。

zh.caption: 图2 一个学出来的维度长什么样。沿某个 AVFS 维度得分最高的一组人脸，上方是人类给出的高频主题词，下方是 CelebA / FairFace 属性——三者独立地指向同一个概念。出于隐私考虑，图中人脸为合成的 StyleGAN3 图像。

zh.text: 论文：https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17176 — 代码：https://github.com/SonyAI/a_view_from_somewhere
为什么人口统计标签是一把错的尺子
类别标签回答的是错误的问题。它至多能告诉你一张脸被归入哪一类，却无法说清同一类里两张脸到底有多相似——而「相似程度」恰恰是多样性审计真正关心的东西。人的外貌是连续变化的，同一张脸在不同观察者眼里也可能不同，因此任何固定标签都是对人类实际感知的一次有损、且忽略观察者视角的压缩。
早先也有工作尝试从人类判断中学习人脸的感知嵌入，但都撞上了两堵墙。一类方法只能安放训练时见过的那些刺激，完全无法为一张新面孔生成嵌入；另一类方法则把所有判断汇成一个「平均观察者」，丢掉了标注者内部与标注者之间的差异——而这份差异恰恰在告诉你：相似与否，取决于是谁在看。AVFS 要做的，是同时穿过这两堵墙。
方法：三选一判断，加上「每人一张」的掩码
数据来自一个「找不同」式的三选一任务（odd-one-out，即 triplet 判断）：看三张脸，标注者挑出与另外两张最不相似的那一张。这逼出的是相对比较而非绝对标签，人做起来也更容易保持一致。关键之处在于，这 638,180 次判断里的每一次，都记录下了做出该判断的标注者身份与其自报的人口统计信息——数据集记下的不只是「判断了什么」，还有「是谁在判断」。

在这份数据之上是一个条件模型。一个 ResNet18 卷积网络把每张脸映射为 128 维的嵌入。每位标注者配有一个可学习的门控向量，经过 sigmoid 后用来缩放每一维嵌入对该标注者的重要程度。两张脸的相似度，就是它们经掩码与整流后的嵌入的点积；模型再据此从一个三元组内的三对相似度中预测「哪张最不像」的概率。写成公式，单个标注者的相似度为 sim_a(i,j) = (σ(φ_a) ⊙ ReLU(w_i)) · (σ(φ_a) ⊙ ReLU(w_j))，其中 φ_a 是标注者 a 的掩码，w_i 是第 i 张脸的嵌入。

两个设计让这个空间不只是「准」，更是「可用」。把所有掩码都置为 1，就去掉了条件、退化为一个统一的无条件空间（AVFS-U）；保留掩码则得到条件版本 AVFS-C 以及事后版本 AVFS-CPH。而一个「稀疏 + 非负」的惩罚项会把大多数维度压到零，只留下约 22 个非负且人能读懂的维度——论文在保留 22 个可解释维度的同时，验证准确率达到 61.9%。上方的图2 就展示了其中一个维度：它得分最高的人脸、人类用来描述它的词、以及独立对上号的 CelebA/FairFace 属性三者一致，这正是这里所说的「可解释」。
一个与感知对齐的空间，真的能预测人类判断吗？
第一项测试留出的是模型训练时见过的那批脸上的判断，共 24,060 次，让模型预测人类会把哪张脸选为「最不像」。图1 给出了各模型的准确率。用语义标签训练出的表征（FairFace、CelebA、FFHQ、CASIA-WebFace）都停留在 50% 出头，而 AVFS 系列明显甩开它们；哪怕只用 12.5% 的判断来训练的 AVFS-U 变体，也依然胜过所有语义基线。

zh.caption: 图1 同一批 24,060 张脸上留出判断的相似性预测。语义标签表征（左）落后于每一个 AVFS 模型（右）；即便是 AVFS-U-12.5% 也仍领先于基线。

zh.text: 更难的一关，是在 80,300 次针对全新面孔的判断上测试——这些脸模型在训练中从未见过。如果一个空间只是「记住」了训练样本，到这里就会崩掉。但如图3 所示，AVFS 系列再次领先语义基线，而标注者专属掩码在陌生面孔上依然有效——这说明掩码抓住的是某个人判断相似性的可迁移方式，而不是对训练刺激的死记硬背。

zh.caption: 图3 在 80,300 次全新面孔判断上的相似性预测。条件模型（AVFS-C、AVFS-CPH）能泛化到完全由未见过的脸构成的三元组。

zh.text: 下面这张表把两项测试浓缩到一起。无论是同一批脸还是全新面孔，AVFS 系列相对最强的语义基线都提升了大约六到十二个百分点，而这一切都是在训练全程没见过任何人口统计标签的前提下做到的。

zh.caption: 表1 三选一准确率（%），最强语义基线对比 AVFS 系列。

zh.text: 标注者真的重要吗，还是那张掩码只是摆设？
如果每个人判断相似性的方式都一样，那么标注者掩码就是可互换的，随机打乱也不该有任何代价。作者正是这样做检验：把这 80,300 次全新面孔判断上各自绑定的标注者掩码随机重新分配，再重算准确率，重复 100 次。最强条件模型的准确率从 61.7% 掉到 52.8%——一个幅度大且稳定的下滑，说明标注者并不可互换，「谁在判断」本身就是信号的一部分。
第二项分析逐一剔除嵌入维度。只需 6–13 个维度，就能恢复 95–99% 的预测准确率；但要解释 95–99% 的完整相似性结构，则需要 15–22 个维度。这道差距正是重点所在：哪些维度重要，取决于比较所处的语境——而这恰恰是连续、条件化的空间该捕捉、固定标签却做不到的东西。

zh.caption: 图4 标注者的立场性（positionality）。一个线性 SVM 仅凭掩码就能按人口统计群体把标注者显著区分开（远高于代表随机水平的横线），说明社会文化背景在人们判断人脸相似性时留下了可测量的痕迹。

zh.text: 图4 从另一个方向印证了同一点。一个简单的线性分类器，仅凭标注者的掩码就能按人口统计群体把他们区分开，且每个置信区间都明显高于随机水平。模型从未在这些群体标签上训练过；这种结构之所以浮现，是因为不同的人确实在以不同的方式给各个视觉维度赋权。论文在这里措辞谨慎——这是在描述判断如何因人而异，而不是把任何一种分组当作事实真值来背书。
它的意义
AVFS 用「记录是谁做了哪次判断」换掉了「人口统计标签」，换回一种连续、可解释、与人类感知对齐的人脸表征——它能在不把人塞进离散盒子的前提下衡量多样性。对于在采集敏感属性上受法律与伦理约束的团队来说，这是一个实用的替代方案，而不只是一种哲学立场。
该守住的边界也值得放在眼前：图中人脸都近似正面，标注者群体虽多元却终归有限，因此学到的维度反映的是这一群观察者，而非放之四海皆准的「人类」。但这套框架只需知道「哪次判断出自哪位标注者」，因此它并不专属于人脸——同样的配方，可以为几乎任何建立在人类比较之上的任务学出与感知对齐的表征。正是这份普适性，让这篇论文值得一读。

en.caption: Figure 2. What a learned dimension looks like. The highest-scoring faces along one AVFS dimension, with the human-generated topic labels (top) and the CelebA / FairFace attributes (bottom) that independently line up with it. Faces are synthetic StyleGAN3 images used for privacy.

en.text: The method: odd-one-out judgments and a mask per annotator

The data comes from an odd-one-out task (a triplet judgment): shown three faces, an annotator picks the one least similar to the other two. This forces a relative comparison rather than an absolute label, and it is cognitively easy to do consistently. Crucially, every one of the 638,180 judgments is stamped with the identity and self-reported demographics of the annotator who made it, so the dataset records not just what was judged but who judged it.

On top of this data sits a conditional model. A ResNet18 convnet maps each face to a 128-dimensional embedding. Each annotator is given a learnable gating vector that, after a sigmoid, scales the importance of every embedding dimension for that person. Similarity between two faces is then the dot product of their masked, rectified embeddings, and the model predicts the odd-one-out probability from the three pairwise similarities in a triplet. Formally the per-annotator similarity is sim_a(i,j) = (σ(φ_a) ⊙ ReLU(w_i)) · (σ(φ_a) ⊙ ReLU(w_j)), where φ_a is annotator a's mask and w_i is the embedding of face i.

Two design choices make the space usable rather than just accurate. Setting every mask to ones removes the conditioning and recovers a single unconditional space (AVFS-U); keeping the masks gives the conditional variants AVFS-C and the post-hoc AVFS-CPH. And a sparsity-plus-non-negativity penalty pushes most dimensions to zero, leaving roughly 22 active, non-negative dimensions that a person can actually read — the paper retains 22 interpretable dimensions at 61.9% validation accuracy. Figure 2 above shows one such dimension: its top faces, the words humans used to describe it, and the CelebA/FairFace attributes that independently track it all agree, which is what "interpretable" means here.

en.text: When a team wants to check whether a face dataset is diverse, the reflex is to reach for demographic labels: race, gender, age. It is the default move across the field, and it rests on shaky ground. Those labels are frequently missing, legally restricted to collect, and unreliable the moment a model or a human annotator has to infer them rather than read them off a record.

They also flatten something that is not flat. "Skin tone" collapses into light or dark; two faces filed under the same category can look nothing alike; and rigid taxonomies erase multi-ethnic people and cause real harm when someone is mislabeled. The deeper issue is not a badly chosen taxonomy that a better one would fix. It is the premise that human appearance sorts cleanly into discrete boxes at all.

A View From Somewhere (AVFS), an ICLR 2023 paper from Sony AI and the University of Tokyo, starts from the opposite premise. Instead of labeling faces, it asks people a simpler question: given three faces, which one is the odd one out? The authors collect 638,180 of these judgments over 4,921 faces and learn a continuous embedding space aligned with human perception, with no demographic label anywhere in the training signal.

Does a perception-aligned space actually predict human judgment?

The first test holds out judgments over the same faces the model was trained on — 24,060 of them — and asks the model to predict which face humans called the odd one out. Figure 1 reports accuracy across models. Representations trained on semantic labels (FairFace, CelebA, FFHQ, CASIA-WebFace) sit in the low-to-mid 50% range, while the AVFS models climb well past them; even an AVFS-U variant trained on just 12.5% of the judgments still beats every semantic baseline.

en.text: The harder test uses 80,300 judgments over entirely novel faces the model never saw in training. This is where a merely memorized space would fall apart. en.caption: Figure 3. Predicting similarity on 80,300 judgments over novel faces. The conditional models (AVFS-C, AVFS-CPH) generalize to triplets built entirely from unseen faces.

第一项测试留出的是模型训练时见过的那批脸上的判断，共 24,060 次，让模型预测人类会把哪张脸选为「最不像」。图1 给出了各模型的准确率。用语义标签训练出的表征（FairFace、CelebA、FFHQ、CASIA-WebFace）都停留在 50% 出头，而 AVFS 系列明显甩开它们；哪怕只用 12.5% 的判断来训练的 AVFS-U 变体，也依然胜过所有语义基线。

en.caption: Figure 2. What a learned dimension looks like. The highest-scoring faces along one AVFS dimension, with the human-generated topic labels (top) and the CelebA / FairFace attributes (bottom) that independently line up with it. Faces are synthetic StyleGAN3 images used for privacy.

en.text: Why demographic labels are the wrong measuring stick

Categorical labels answer the wrong question. They can tell you a face is filed as one group or another, but they cannot say how similar two faces within that group are, and similarity is what diversity auditing actually cares about. Human appearance varies continuously, and the same face can strike two observers differently, so any fixed label is a lossy, observer-blind compression of what people actually perceive.

Earlier work tried to learn perceptual embeddings of faces from human judgments, but ran into two walls. Some methods can only place the exact stimuli they were trained on and cannot embed a new face at all. Others pool every judgment into one average observer, discarding the variation within and between annotators — precisely the signal that tells you similarity depends on who is looking. AVFS is designed to break through both walls at once.

zh.caption: 图2 一个学出来的维度长什么样。沿某个 AVFS 维度得分最高的一组人脸，上方是人类给出的高频主题词，下方是 CelebA / FairFace 属性——三者独立地指向同一个概念。出于隐私考虑，图中人脸为合成的 StyleGAN3 图像。

zh.text: 它的意义
AVFS 用「记录是谁做了哪次判断」换掉了「人口统计标签」，换回一种连续、可解释、与人类感知对齐的人脸表征——它能在不把人塞进离散盒子的前提下衡量多样性。对于在采集敏感属性上受法律与伦理约束的团队来说，这是一个实用的替代方案，而不只是一种哲学立场。
该守住的边界也值得放在眼前：图中人脸都近似正面，标注者群体虽多元却终归有限，因此学到的维度反映的是这一群观察者，而非放之四海皆准的「人类」。但这套框架只需知道「哪次判断出自哪位标注者」，因此它并不专属于人脸——同样的配方，可以为几乎任何建立在人类比较之上的任务学出与感知对齐的表征。正是这份普适性，让这篇论文值得一读。

en.caption: Figure 1. Predicting similarity on held-out judgments over the same 24,060 faces. Semantic-label representations (left) trail every AVFS model (right); even AVFS-U-12.5% stays ahead of the baselines.

en.text: The method: odd-one-out judgments and a mask per annotator

The data comes from an odd-one-out task (a triplet judgment): shown three faces, an annotator picks the one least similar to the other two. This forces a relative comparison rather than an absolute label, and it is cognitively easy to do consistently. Crucially, every one of the 638,180 judgments is stamped with the identity and self-reported demographics of the annotator who made it, so the dataset records not just what was judged but who judged it.

On top of this data sits a conditional model. A ResNet18 convnet maps each face to a 128-dimensional embedding. Each annotator is given a learnable gating vector that, after a sigmoid, scales the importance of every embedding dimension for that person. Similarity between two faces is then the dot product of their masked, rectified embeddings, and the model predicts the odd-one-out probability from the three pairwise similarities in a triplet. Formally the per-annotator similarity is sim_a(i,j) = (σ(φ_a) ⊙ ReLU(w_i)) · (σ(φ_a) ⊙ ReLU(w_j)), where φ_a is annotator a's mask and w_i is the embedding of face i.

Two design choices make the space usable rather than just accurate. Setting every mask to ones removes the conditioning and recovers a single unconditional space (AVFS-U); keeping the masks gives the conditional variants AVFS-C and the post-hoc AVFS-CPH. And a sparsity-plus-non-negativity penalty pushes most dimensions to zero, leaving roughly 22 active, non-negative dimensions that a person can actually read — the paper retains 22 interpretable dimensions at 61.9% validation accuracy. Figure 2 above shows one such dimension: its top faces, the words humans used to describe it, and the CelebA/FairFace attributes that independently track it all agree, which is what "interpretable" means here.

en.text: Why it matters

AVFS trades a demographic label for a record of who judged what, and gets back a continuous, interpretable, perception-aligned face representation that measures diversity without forcing people into discrete boxes. For teams constrained by law and ethics on collecting sensitive attributes, that is a practical alternative, not just a philosophical one.

The boundaries are worth keeping in view: the faces are near-frontal and the annotator pool, though diverse, is finite. But the framework only needs to know who made which judgment, so nothing about it is specific to faces — the same recipe could learn perception-aligned representations for almost any task built on human comparison. That generality is what makes the paper worth reading.
